zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, supplied package subset; CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the diplomatic text.

lines.note: Gakugyo is the activity of learning, expressed by manabu shiwaza. The stray, vertically distorted ink after the long-o type is not a secure question mark; the reading Gacuguiǒ agrees with the supplied NINJAL index. Aprẽ continues as der below without a supplied hyphen.
Der completes aprẽder, 'to learn'; estudar offers 'to study' as the alternative. The isolated marks at the far right are not a second text fragment.
Gacuji denotes a learned man, matching both manabu votto and letrado. The damaged initial is G, not the OCR sequence Cr; the printed votto is retained rather than normalized.
Gakumon is study or learning; bun wo manabu explains studying letters. The scan gives Gacumon, without the spurious i of Giacumon.
Ou sciencia completes the gloss with 'or knowledge/science'; this is a continuation of Gacumon, not a separate entry.
Gakumonja is a student or learned person. The Portuguese preserves both stages or senses rather than restricting the word to a modern professional scholar.
Gakumonjo is a place for study. The final jo distinguishes the location from the preceding person-word in ja.
Gakumonso names an herb described as useful for the ailment specified below. The open long-o mark and the printed ß in aßi are retained; no botanical species is inferred.
Sarna identifies the herb's stated use against scabies or a similar skin complaint. X. is the dictionary's regional label and is upright, not part of the italic disease name.
This Gacunin is a musician, explained by gaku no hito. The Portuguese tange- continues into the word for players of instruments.
Dores completes tangedores: players of musical instruments. It belongs to the musical Gacunin rather than the next homographic entry.
The second Gacunin is a learner or student, explicitly distinguished by manabu hito. The separate physical entry is retained despite identical headword spelling.
Gakuki is a musical instrument; gaku no utsuwamono supplies the Japanese paraphrase. The extra OCR C in GCacuqi has no independent type in the scan.
To completes instrumento. The example gakuki wo totonoyuru concerns putting instruments in tune or order, as the next line confirms.
Temperar means tuning the musical instruments here, not tempering materials. It translates the Japanese example on the preceding row.
Gacurio denotes fellow students, with manabu tomo explaining companions in study. No long-vowel mark is supplied to the printed headword.
Discipulos completes condiscipulos, fellow pupils. This short line finishes the preceding gloss.

runs.text: Cabeça, ou principal em couſas de

lines.note: Gakuto is the head or chief in the musical activities specified below. Its printed circumflex is distinct from the carons elsewhere on the page.
Completes the musical-leadership sense and introduces a second sense. Item begins the explanation of leadership among Buddhist clerics rather than another Japanese headword.

runs.text: Cabeça, ou ſuperior principal entre os Bonzos

lines.note: The second sense is the chief or principal superior among a named group of Buddhist clerics. The group-name is deferred to the next physical line.
Xǒdǒ is embedded in the Portuguese phrase 'called Xǒdǒ' and is printed upright. Both long-o marks appear as carons; the Japanese term is recorded for optional whole-word typeface review.
Gakutoku is having acquired learning, paraphrased by manabi uru. The gloss emphasizes attainment rather than simply the ongoing act of study.
The alternative is having received instruction or doctrine. This continues the acquired-learning sense of Gacutocu.
Gakusha is a learned or wise person. The printed x is the ordinary Jesuit spelling here and does not call for modernization.
Gacuxǒ is assigned the same meaning as Gacuxa by Idem. The visible caron is preserved without assimilating it to the neighboring Gacutô circumflex.
Gakushu combines learning with practice; the paraphrase manabi shusuru is completed semantically by the next Portuguese row.

Por por obra means 'put into practice': the first por functions as the verb and the second as the preposition. The repeated printed word is meaningful historical Portuguese, not an OCR duplication to delete.
Gakuya is the place where performers dress. The abbreviated reueſtẽ is preserved, including its tilde, rather than expanded to a modern spelling.

runs.text: ou donde ſaem as figuras do auto.

lines.note: The same room is described as the place from which the play's characters or performers emerge. This makes the theatrical, backstage meaning explicit.

Gakuyu again denotes companions in study. The small mark over final u remains faint after both scan passes; the supplied caron reading Gacuyǔ is retained rather than substituted with an unmarked vowel.
Estudo completes 'fellow pupils in study'. The scan supports u, not the OCR's a in eſtado; the latter would change the meaning to a state or condition.

runs.text: Contenda ou porfia em algũa duuida,

lines.note: Gadocu describes a dispute or stubborn contention over a doubt or question. The tilde is placed over u in algũa, as printed.

runs.text: & opinião com outro inſiſtindo cada hum com

lines.note: The dispute is with another person, each insisting on his own opinion. The sentence continues into the manner of that insistence below.
Each person maintains his view spiritedly or obstinately. Gadocuni suru exemplifies behaving in this contentious fashion; Vt belongs to the italic apparatus.

Gafacu is here an excellent poet, explained as someone skilled in poetry. The damaged internal i in Xijcano is compatible with the supplied reading; the entry must not be reinterpreted from a modern painter-related sense of gahaku.
Gafameqi describes moving in the hasty, noisy fashion explained below. The headword begins G, not C; the abbreviated principal forms remain unexpanded.

runs.text: fazer algũa couſa com preßa, & eſtrondo, ou

lines.note: The action is performed with haste and noise. The scan's preßa is retained rather than replaced by a modern spelling or a conjectured alternative s-sequence.
Desatentadamente adds heedless or distracted action to the preceding description. It is a complete short continuation, not an independent adverb entry.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de cair de ſubito, ou

lines.note: Gafato is labeled an adverb and introduces sudden falling or movement. Adu. belongs to the italic Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: de ſe aleuantar, ou de fazer algũa couſa que ſe

lines.note: The scope includes getting up or performing an unexpected action. The relative clause continues on the next row.
The action is unexpected and sudden. The scan supports Gafato, not the OCR's Garato; the closely printed nãoeſperaua is kept joined rather than given an editorial word-space.
Vochita completes the example 'fell suddenly'. The next example begins with Gafato vo- and its visible dividing hyphen is retained.
Qita completes voqita, 'got up', and the Portuguese explicitly translates sudden rising. Itẽ introduces an additional sense and retains the abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Modo de diſcrepar, ou faltar em algũa promeſ

lines.note: The additional sense concerns failing or departing from a promise or expectation. Promeſ continues into ſa below; no unseen line-end hyphen is supplied.

runs.text: ſa, ou outra couſa que hum eſperaua. Vt,

lines.note: Completes promessa and extends the sense to anything someone expected. Vt introduces the Japanese example on the next line.
Gafato chigǒta describes an outcome differing unexpectedly from what one supposed. The clear caron in chigǒta and the printed division diſ- are preserved.
Crepou completes discrepou, 'differed' or 'failed to agree'. It ends the column's Gafato entry; there is no further body fragment below it.
Gafô is one's own religious teaching or sect, explained by waga ho. Both visible o-marks are circumflexes; Bup. is an upright Buddhist-domain label.
Gagacu denotes one's own enlightenment or understanding, paraphrased by waga satori. The Buddhist label is upright and the example is physically divided after Gaga-.
Cu completes Gagacu. The example is explained as knowing naturally without learning; the printed fonpuxǒ is retained, with the final caron, rather than normalized from Buddhist terminology.
Completes aprender and adds 'without reasoning, as Xaca said of himself'. Xaca is a Japanese name embedded within Portuguese and is set upright; it is not an independent headword.
Gagan is equated with Ieni, money or cash; Portuguese caixas here refers to the coins, not modern packing boxes. Initial consonantal I in Ieni is retained.

runs.text: Certa feição de ſerra de carpinteiros

lines.note: Gagari names a particular form of carpenter's saw. The following row supplies the direction in which it cuts the timber.

runs.text: com que abrem algum pao ao comprido.

lines.note: The saw is used to open or split a piece of wood lengthwise. This is the functional continuation of the Gagari definition.
The example describes a lofty, steep rock; Gagataru qualifies ganjeqi rather than naming the rock itself. Ro- begins the Portuguese rochedo.
Completes rochedo, 'a very high and steep rocky mass'. The description fixes the sense of the preceding Japanese expression.
Gai is explained by korosu, 'kill', and Gaisuru supplies the verbal use. The long s in Coroſu and Gaiſuru is retained rather than confused with f.
Gai wo maneku means inviting harm or death. The Portuguese begins 'provoke or seek', with its object continuing on the next row.
The object is death. The example begins 'raising a tiger, oneself...' and preserves the historical form yaxinǒte and the division of mizzucara across rows.
Ra completes mizzucara; the example describes bringing harm upon oneself. Taif. is the upright citation label, while Lib. 36. is italic bibliographic apparatus.

runs.text: Criai o coruo, & tirar vos ha o olho, aßi criã

lines.note: The Portuguese compares the tiger example to raising a crow that will take out one's eye. Criã continues as do below; the OCR's final p has no printed letter to support it.

runs.text: do ao tigre he grangear a morte.

lines.note: Completes criando and explains that raising the tiger is procuring one's own death. The printed grangear is retained without modernizing its spelling.

runs.text: Preſunção, ou proprio parecer em que hũ

lines.note: This separate Gai means presumption or the personal judgment in which someone trusts. It is not the killing-related entry above; hũ retains the abbreviation tilde.
The example describes arranging matters according to one's own judgment. Or- begins ordenar and Vt remains italic.

runs.text: denar, ou fazer algũa couſa por ſeu proprio pa

lines.note: Completes ordenar and explains doing something by one's own opinion. Pa continues into parecer without adding an unprinted dividing hyphen.
Completes parecer and adds personal will. The final point visible after vontade is restored.
Gaibyo is a coughing or catarrhal illness, paraphrased by shiwabuki no yamai. The Portuguese reads Cadarrão, not OCR Cadamão; the doubled r and historical d are retained.
Gaibyo wo okosu means beginning to develop the illness. The headword is repeated with ai, not OCR Ghibiǒuo; the printed ater remains joined and catar- carries a visible hyphen.
Ro completes catarro, followed by an example meaning to suffer from the illness. Eſtar has long s, not the meaning-destroying OCR f; doen- continues below.
Completes doente de catarro, 'ill with catarrh'. It translates the preceding vazzurǒ example.
Gaibun is an adverb equated with zuibun and glossed as acting with care. Adu. is italic apparatus, whereas the Japanese synonym and its i, marker remain upright.
Adds diligence to the adverbial gloss. The short continuation belongs to Gaibun.

Gaikaku denotes an impressive outward appearance or scale, illustrated by large structures below. The provisional short-s spelling in Mostra is retained rather than globally reclassifying its st type.
The gloss lists works, houses and enclosures. The example begins with the alternatives 'large' and, on the next row, 'wide'; l is the alternative marker, not a Japanese word.
Hiroi gaikaku completes the example of great extent or imposing appearance. The Portuguese is vulto, not OCR vulio; the t is supported by the scan and the architectural context.
Specifies that the bulk or appearance belongs to a building, enclosure and similar structures. This completes Gaicacu rather than introducing another noun.

Gaichǔ is illustrated by a time-related expression and paraphrased as toki no uchi. The final mark in the headword is a caron; the first marked u in Iǔnigaichǔ is faint and remains a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.
Chi completes uchi, 'within'; the Portuguese gives 'within the hour'. S. is the upright written-register label, not part of the italic translation.
Gaikot denotes the bones of a dead body. Oſſada has two long-s types, not two f letters; the bare final t of the Japanese headword is preserved.
Gaina or gaina mono describes a free, self-willed person. The Portuguese a- begins amiga on the next row; the alternatives stay within one entry.

runs.text: miga de ſeu parecer, pouco cortes pera com o ſe

lines.note: The person favors his own opinion and shows little courtesy toward the people listed next. Se continues into senhor without an invented hyphen.
Completes senhor and lists lord, father and mother as those toward whom courtesy is lacking. Historical pay and mãy are retained.
Gaiqi is again catarrh, with an example of having the illness. The Portuguese division Eſ- is visible and the long s is kept.
Completes estar doente de cadarrão, being ill with catarrh. The repeated d spelling is preserved rather than normalized to modern catarro.

runs.text: Filho de galo da China, & galinha de

lines.note: Gairi denotes offspring of a Chinese cock and a Japanese hen. The gloss continues with the hen's origin on the next physical row.

Completes the parentage and gives the regional label X. The cross-reference directs the reader to gayeri; Idẽ Vide is italic, while the Japanese reference target is upright and marked for optional whole-word typeface review.
Gaisai denotes a boundary or limit, paraphrased by the repeated kiwa. The repetition is printed and is not collapsed.
Gaiso is a cough. The scan supports the printed Xuabuqi, even though the longer Xiuabuqi appears above; no vowel is supplied to harmonize the two forms.
Gaito is glossed as a crossroads. The closed long-o mark is kept distinct from the neighboring caroned forms.
Gaixi gives the verb meaning 'kill' with abbreviated principal forms. The comma-separated forms belong to one entry and remain unexpanded.
Gaishin is a cruel or murderous heart, paraphrased by korosu kokoro. The Portuguese description continues below.
The heart is also described as treacherous. Gaishin wo okosu begins an example of manifesting this cruel intention; Mo- starts mostrar-se.
Completes mostrar-se cruel and adds hatred. Gaixinuo begins a second example whose continuation was omitted from the baseline and is restored as c2-l047a.

The restored final body row completes Gaixinuo with the alternatives sashihasamu and fukumu, harboring a murderous intention. The enlarged scan shows two separate commas after ſaxifaſamu, both retained. The Portuguese gloss continues on f232; the lower-right coração is a separate catchword.
